title: Forage: mini-sprint notes — contextuality, probes, and quick experiments
summary: A short, loose notebook from a 48h sprint aimed at rapid foraging through papers/blogs and turning quick hypotheses into tiny probes. Goal: identify 2–3 actionable experiments to run on Redwood infra that might inform KV-cache heuristics and prompt-scheduling defaults.
content:
Topline: this is intentionally scrappy. I spent two days skimming ~12 papers and 6 blog posts, then translated a few recurring claims into 4 tiny probes. Notes below are half paper-summaries, half my thought process and runnable ideas.

Motivation / hypothesis cluster:
- Many recent papers claim apparent contextual robustness when models see repeated context patterns or local coherence. Practical upshot: if we can detect compact repetitions we might avoid full KV-cache inflation and instead keep a lightweight 'snippet index' per request.
- Secondary: quantized models often retain surface-level pattern recall but lose fine-grained calibration; probe behavior differs by head/kv distribution. That suggests cheaper probes (few-shot token-level tests) could detect when we should fall back to higher-precision kernels.

What I read (very quick takes):
- "Scattered Context Patterns and Local Stability" (paper, small transformer study): argument is that local repetition stabilizes next-token distribution quickly. Converges in ~6 tokens for many synthetic sequences. Implication: we can detect stabilization windows and reduce prefix re-eval frequency.
- Blog: "When KV caches lie" (engineering post): anecdotal cases where cache eviction policies produce hallucination-causing prefix mismatches. Emphasis on mismatch detection heuristics (e.g., token entropy spikes).
- ArXiv note on probing quantized attention matrices: shows a few attention patterns become noisy when switching from fp16->int8; noise manifests as higher variance in top-k attention mass.
- Conference slide: "microbenchmarks for shorter tail SLOs" — argues for surge-loading small requests and measuring token-tail latency. Worth stealing ideas for our microprobe harness.

Few high-level synthesis points:
1) Detection beats perfect prediction. If we can cheaply detect when the model state is 'stable' or 'noisy', we can change execution mode (compact kv, low-precision, or fallback to fp16) instead of trying to predict the next tokens perfectly.
2) Cheap probes can be cheap heuristics: e.g., 8-token synthetic probe inserted after prefix to measure entropy drift.
3) We should be paranoid about adversarial prefixes — probes must be robust to prompt engineering by customers. Keep probes opt-in or clearly documented.

Mini-probes to implement (prioritized):
- Probe A — "stabilization window estimation": insert a 8-token synthetic suffix drawn from a small deterministic template (e.g., repeating short phrases) and measure how quickly token distribution concentrates. Metric: average token perplexity drop between positions 1 and 6. Thresholds: if drop > 30% -> mark prefix as "stable". Cost: one forward pass with small target length.
- Probe B — "kv-noise sniff": run a lightweight attention top-k mass estimator on quantized kernel path (int8) vs small fp16 baseline on a short 4-token probe. Metric: variance(top_k_mass) across heads. High variance = likely noisy quantization. Action: route this request to fp16 or increase beam temperature.
- Probe C — "entropy spike detector": compute token-level entropy for the first 6 tokens of the user prompt (no extra generation). If entropy spike > X relative to baseline distribution for that model -> consider enabling conservative fallback (e.g., smaller decoding step).
- Probe D — "cache-shift sentinel": on reused conversation contexts, materialize two KV prefixes offset by last-turn boundary and compare logit similarity on a tiny clamped prompt. If similarity drops below threshold -> trigger cache refresh.

Notes on cost and SLO impact:
- Each probe is <0.5ms for small models, ~1-3ms for medium; still inline they add tail risk. Run them in parallel on a copy of the request if we can (off-main-path), otherwise only for prioritized customers (experiment).
- Prefer warm kernels for probes; cold-probe variance will swamp signal. Keep in mind dedicated pools advantage here.

Experiment plan (quick):
1) Implement Probe A + logging in a dev branch. Instrument: model id, quantization flag, prompt length, probe metric, response latencies, downstream reroute decision.
2) Run 10k sampled real session prefixes (anonymized) on dev cluster with probes enabled. Collect metric distribution and correlate with observed generation perplexities and user-visible regressions (if any).
3) If signal strong -> A/B test enabling lightweight stabilization-based compact-kv mode for 5% of traffic on Dedicated pool. Monitor token cost and 95/99/995 latency.

Open questions / risks:
- Privacy/regulatory: inserting probes modifies request payload (albeit transient). Need to flag this in docs and possibly make probe synthetic text non-leaking. Option: run probes purely on internals (cache state) without appending tokens to user-visible prompt.
- Adversarial prompts could game detection. Consider opt-in for customer-managed probes or only enable for internal workloads initially.
- Interaction with function-calling or structured output flows — probes must be conditional and aware of callouts.

Quick implementation checklist (TODO):
- [ ] Prototype Probe A in python harness + toy model (llama-quant) — estimate latency cost per model family. (owner: me)
- [ ] Add telemetry schema: probe_type, probe_result, model_variant, kernel_path, reroute_decision. (owner: Ravi)
- [ ] Draft design note for legal/ops on probe privacy considerations. (owner: Ava)
- [ ] Small A/B config gated on customer tier. (owner: eng-delivery)

Random micro-observations from reading session:
- Some authors recommend using 'reconstruction loss' on a small heldout token set as a proxy for calibration. Might be heavier but good for offline analysis.
- Entropy heuristics are cheap but sensitive to tokenization choices; run token-length-normalized metrics.
- For quant noise sniff, head-wise aggregation matters: median per-head is more robust than mean.

Thoughts on naming and doc flow: call the experiment 'forage-probes' to emphasize small cheap checks. Keep default behavior conservative: no probe-driven reroutes without human-validated thresholds.

Appendix: Useful links I skimmed (notes to self)
- short paper: "Local stabilization in transformers" (TODO: cite when finalizing)
- eng blog: "KV cache lies" (engineering blog; search internal)
- slides: Microbenchmarks for tail SLOs (internal slides share)

Endnote: this doc is messy; intention is to capture my foraging path and the handful of probes that felt immediately implementable. Next step: spin up Probe A on a small dev cluster and come back with numbers.

Contact: ping me in #eng-applied-ml or drop a quick thread in #forage-probes for follow-ups.

Notes to self (one-line reminders):
- keep probes outside customer-visible tokens if possible
- prefer median head-aggr for sniffing
- document probe opt-in/opt-out in API docs
